h1: The 6 Best TP-Link Network Switches of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six TP-Link switches from a 5-port Gigabit to a 48-port managed PoE+ model, compared on speed, PoE budget, ports and warranty.
summary: The TP-Link TL-SG105 is the best switch for most desks, five Gigabit ports with QoS and a three-year warranty under $25. The TL-SG1005P adds four PoE+ ports. The TL-SG105S-M2 and TL-SG108S-M2 bring 2.5G, the TL-SG116 offers 16 Gigabit ports, and the TL-SG3452P is a managed 48-port PoE+ rack switch for large installs.
intro: Most people shopping for a network switch count ports and stop. The number that actually limits you is the speed of each port. A Gigabit switch quietly throttles a 2.5G internet plan or a 2.5G NAS, and a switch without PoE cannot power a camera no matter how many ports it has. Port count is cheap to fix later; speed and power are not.

Six TP-Link switches are ranked here from spec sheets, weighing port speed, PoE budget, port count, management features and warranty length, and we checked what each listing states rather than benchmarking throughput. They run from a five-port Gigabit box under $25 to a 48-port managed PoE+ rack unit, so the order puts general usefulness first and size or specialization last.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: The plug-and-play five-port switch that fits most desks.
products.description:
The TL-SG105 is the switch to buy when you just need more wired ports. It has five Gigabit ports with QoS and IGMP snooping, a metal desktop or wall-mount case and a three-year warranty, under $25. QoS lets it prioritize traffic, and IGMP snooping stops multicast streams, such as IPTV, from flooding every port.

It ranks first because it covers the most common need at the lowest price. The 2.5G models below are faster but cost more, and they only help when the rest of your gear is also 2.5G.

Buy it for a desk or a small TV cabinet. The caveat is the ceiling: every port is capped at Gigabit, so a 2.5G router or NAS will be held back, and there is no PoE, so cameras and access points need their own power adapters.
products.idealFor: Desks and small setups with Gigabit gear.
products.skipIf: You have a 2.5G plan or devices.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG1005P 5-Port Gigabit PoE Switch
products.verdict: Powers four PoE+ devices from one box with 65W total.
products.description:
The TL-SG1005P adds power to the same formula. It has four PoE+ ports sharing 65W in total, plus one uplink, with QoS, IGMP snooping and a three-year warranty, in the $25 to $50 bracket. PoE carries power and data over one cable, which means a camera or access point needs only a cable run, not a nearby outlet.

It ranks second because it extends the TL-SG105 idea into PoE, but the limit is the budget: 65W is shared, so four hungry devices can exceed it.

Best for a few cameras or one access point. Check each device's wattage against the 65W total before buying. The caveat is the layout: one port is a plain uplink, so you have only four powered ports, and all of them share the same budget.
products.idealFor: Small camera or access point setups.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 5-Port 2.5G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Five 2.5G ports that run over existing Cat5e cabling.
products.description:
The TL-SG105S-M2 is the cheapest way to go beyond Gigabit. It has five ports at 2.5G with 25Gbps switching capacity in a compact metal case, works over existing Cat5e cabling and sits in the $25 to $50 bracket. Capacity matters because a switch must carry every port's traffic at once, and 25Gbps covers five 2.5G ports in both directions with room to spare.

It ranks third because 2.5G only pays off with matching gear. Against the TL-SG105 it costs more but removes the Gigabit ceiling.

Buy it if your router, NAS or PC already has a 2.5G port. The caveat is that it has no PoE, so cameras still need separate power, and if everything else you own is Gigabit, the extra spending buys nothing.
products.idealFor: Anyone with a 2.5G router or NAS.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 8-Port 2.5G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Eight fanless 2.5G ports for a growing multi-device setup.
products.description:
The TL-SG108S-M2 extends the idea to eight ports. It has eight ports at 2.5G with 40Gbps capacity, a fanless unmanaged design and Cat5e compatibility, in the $50 to $100 bracket. Fanless means no moving parts and no noise, which matters if the switch sits on a desk or in a living room cabinet.

It ranks fourth because it is the same concept as the five-port 2.5G model with more ports and a higher bracket. You pay for headroom you may not use.

Best for a home lab with several 2.5G devices, such as a NAS, a workstation and a mini PC. The caveat is plain: do not buy it for only two or three devices, since the five-port model covers that. It has no PoE or management either.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG116 16-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Sixteen Gigabit ports for a crowded closet.
products.description:
The TL-SG116 trades speed for volume. It has 16 Gigabit ports with QoS and IGMP snooping, a 0 to 40 degree operating range and a three-year warranty, in the $50 to $100 bracket. In a house with consoles, TVs, desktops and printers all on cables, sixteen ports means everything connects without a second switch.

It ranks fifth because it offers volume rather than speed, and the 2.5G switches above are faster per port. It has no PoE either.

Best for a wired home with many devices. The 0 to 40 degree range matters in a warm closet, where a switch with a narrower range can overheat. The caveat is that every port is capped at Gigabit, so it will not suit a 2.5G plan.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG3452P 48-Port L2+ Managed PoE Switch
products.verdict: A 48-port managed PoE+ switch for large installs.
products.description:
The TL-SG3452P is a different class of equipment. It has 48 PoE+ ports sharing 384W, L2+ management, four SFP slots, static routing and a five-year warranty, in the $500 and up bracket. Management lets you create VLANs and control traffic, and 384W of PoE budget can power dozens of cameras and phones.

It ranks last for a general audience because it is far more switch than a home needs. For a business or large lab, it leads the list on features.

Buy it for offices and campuses where someone will configure it. The caveat is cost and complexity: a home user would pay for ports and management they never use, and the setup takes network knowledge. Everyone else should choose a smaller unmanaged model.
products.idealFor: Offices and large installs needing management.

whatMatters.detail: Port speed is the maximum data rate per port, either 1Gbps or 2.5Gbps here. A Gigabit switch caps a faster router or NAS no matter how large its total capacity. Check the listing for the per-port speed, not only the total switching capacity, and match it to your fastest device, because the slowest link in a chain sets the real speed.

PoE sends power over the Ethernet cable. The total budget is shared across ports, so 65W covers a few devices but not many. Add up each device's wattage before buying, and leave a margin of at least ten percent, since devices can draw more at startup. The TL-SG1005P has 65W for four ports, while the TL-SG3452P has 384W across 48.

Unmanaged switches work on plug-in with no setup. Managed switches add routing and VLAN control through a web interface. Most homes do not need management, and a managed unit costs more and needs configuring. Check the listing for the word managed or L2+ before assuming simplicity, and remember a managed switch is wasted money in most homes.

Buy a few more ports than you need today. Extra ports cost little, but replacing a full switch costs more, and a crowded switch has no room for a new console or camera. Count every wired device, including TVs and printers, then add two or three spares for future gear, such as a streaming box or a second desk.

Warranties here run from 3 to 5 years, and a metal case and fanless design help with heat and noise. Check both on the listing. A fanless metal case is quiet in a living room, and the operating temperature range matters in a closet or a garage, where heat builds up quietly.

faq.q: Will a 2.5G switch work with Gigabit devices?
faq.a: Our listings do not cover this in detail, but 2.5G switches generally negotiate lower speeds. Check the listing to confirm backward compatibility with your Gigabit gear before buying.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with switches?
faq.a: Overbuying ports or ignoring speed. Match port speed to your fastest device, and buy PoE only if you have cameras or access points to power, not as an extra, because PoE ports cost more per port.

faq.q: Is the TL-SG1005P worth it over the TL-SG105?
faq.a: Yes if you have PoE devices, thanks to four PoE+ ports at 65W total. If not, the TL-SG105 is cheaper and does the same switching with a lower price and a smaller footprint.

faq.q: Do I need new cables for 2.5G?
faq.a: The 2.5G models here are listed as working over existing Cat5e cabling, so you may not need to rewire, which saves time in a finished house. Damaged or very long cables may still limit the speed, so test the cable if you see only Gigabit links.

faq.q: How do I keep a switch cool?
faq.a: Give it airflow and avoid stacking it under other equipment or inside a closed cabinet without ventilation. The TL-SG116 lists a 0 to 40 degree C operating range, which suits most rooms but not a hot attic.

faq.q: Can the SG3452P be used at home?
faq.a: It can, but it is built for large installs with 48 PoE+ ports and management. Most homes will pay for ports and features they never use, so pick the TL-SG116 instead unless you truly need management or a large PoE budget.

finalTake: Buy the TL-SG105 unless a device you own already runs faster than Gigabit or needs power. Choose the TL-SG1005P for cameras and access points, the TL-SG105S-M2 or TL-SG108S-M2 for 2.5G gear, and the TL-SG116 for a crowded closet. The TL-SG3452P belongs in offices, not homes.
